I have a lot of experience with moving a child around because my former partner was in academia. You and your child would enjoy what I did: lots of dislocation without the support of military benefits and social structure. Yes, we got to see the country and had many unforgettable experiences, but you can get the same by vacationing. It really hurt both my child and I to keep saying good-bye to friends, to have to abandon community and places we had grown attached to, to have to keep finding new doctors and dentists and schools all over again. Fortunately, my child turned out to have very strong social skills, so he always managed to make new friends. Many kids are not so lucky and would struggle a lot more and end up being socially isolated.

Small children, and boys in particular, need space to run around and act like the little monkeys that they are. They deserve a living situation which is appropriate to this need where they won't end up breaking things and getting yelled at a lot. They need parks and playgrounds and they need friends in those spaces, because playing even with a cool, fun parent isn't ever going to be the same. They need to have things like bikes and skateboards and basketballs, and these things are going to get dusty and dirty, because children need physical, unstructured play.

Kids also need a certain amount of toys and art supplies. Whereas I agree wholeheartedly that many modern children have too many toys, it is normal for kids to develop interests, which may be intense. Some of these interests will fade quickly but some of these will develop into lifelong interests. Toys and play develop a child's mind and imagination, and playing with their friends develops a child's social skills. I learned about math and reading diagrams playing with blocks and building sets. Both my child and I spent much of our childhoods building elaborate imaginary cities with people, buildings, cars, trains, and airports, and both alone and with our friends, concocted ongoing and complex dramas of crime, natural disasters, attacking monsters, international intrigue, and noble sorrows and grand tragedies. You need a box of toys to really get that going.

Kids need books. Sure, you can cycle out the books they've outgrown as you acquire new ones, and you can rely largely on your local bookstore, public library, or the Internet, but young children find tremendous comfort in re-reading certain beloved books over a number of years, and older children deserve to enjoy having a favorite book or two that is all their own--an encyclopedia of reptiles and amphibians, a bilingual picture dictionary, a book of sports cars or WWII airplanes--whatever your child loves and finds continuity in.

Kids need a place to do their homework. That place needs things like a stapler, glue, markers or crayons, pens and pencils, a pencil sharpener, and scissors. They need enough space to put the poster board flat and still have some room for the supplies when they're working on that project on volcanoes or historical figures. You need room for a laptop and a printer and a backup drive with daily backups for that inevitable day when he spills his drink all over the laptop.

To live in a tiny house, you need to be tidy and organized. You can't let the dishes just go; you can't let the laundry pile up. You have to curate your possessions ruthlessly. You have to organize your papers perfectly so that you can locate your important documents at a moment's notice. Most adults have to work at developing this skill. It is the rare child who has the remotest interest in this skill, let alone the capacity for it.

In short, this is how I see it. In the past, kids lived in simple structures in the woods or communal living situations, but this is not the past. Those kids of history were living in an environment in which everybody else was in similar conditions, so they were adapted to that. Some of those kids were made stronger in some sense, but many did not thrive.

Your son lives in a day and age and culture in which his companions will be watching TV, playing with toys, participating in sports, riding their bikes, and playing video games. My unscientific impression, gleaned from reading and anecdotes, is that such children tended to resent the isolation that comes from feeling weird and out of it.

So you can't control your sibling, and you can't make your parents fix this. They are clearly overwhelmed and aren't going to change what they are doing either. It's up to them to make whatever choices they make, and you have zero control over that.

All you can control is yourself. You don't have to put up with your sibling's aggression. I don't recommend that you ignore it. One thing you can try is to speak to them in a calm moment. Tell them that you are proud of all they've accomplished with picking a sport and sticking to it. Tell them you wish you two could have a better relationship, and express that you feel hurt and angry when they comment on your eating choices and your body. Assure them that you promise not to talk about their eating choices or their health with your parents, and that you recognize that it's their business. Ask them if that seems like a fair deal, and stick with it. Finally, tell them that you care about them, you just want them to have a healthy and happy life, and that you hope you can have a better relationship before you leave home.

Going forward, resist the temptation to criticize their eating or exercise either to them or your parents. Hopefully, this may mitigate their impulse to retaliate by criticizing you. If they do criticize you, remind them of your deal, and ask them not to worry about the choices you make with food and your body, just as you are not criticizing them to your parents anymore. Then if they persist, leave the room, even if the whole family is at dinner. If they follow you or keep at it, leave the house and take a walk.

Maybe you're already doing this, but you may want to spend more time out of the house doing outside activities, such as working, volunteering, finding a social hobby or club, and spending time with your friends.

**TL;DR:** You have no influence over your sibling's eating choices, health, or your parents' reaction to them. You can control yourself and your own reactions. Refuse to put up with nagging or bullying from your sibling. Find things to do outside of your home.
